title: The two parse paths
caption: Ordinary files go straight to OXC. TSRX files are scanned, projected, parsed once, then handed back as the tree you actually wrote.

nodes.ordinary: Ordinary JavaScript and TypeScript skip every TSRX step and take the direct public-OXC path, exactly like oxc-parser.
nodes.tsrx: A .tsrx parse starts with the exact bytes you wrote.
nodes.scan: One linear scan finds every TSRX control and records where it starts and ends, while protecting strings, comments, templates, and JSX text.
nodes.projection: The TSRX controls become legal TSX placeholders in a temporary in-memory copy; your code is copied in byte-for-byte unchanged.
nodes.parser: Canonical OXC parses the original ordinary source or the projected copy exactly once.
nodes.reconstruct: The projected tree is rebuilt into the tree you authored: TSRX controls come back as their own node types, and every span points at your original bytes.
nodes.results: The result exposes program, module, comments, and errors as independent lazy getters, so you only pay for the fields you read.

steps.label: Ordinary files
steps.caption: A .ts or .tsx file goes straight to the canonical OXC parser, the same road oxc-parser takes.

steps.label: Scan and project
steps.caption: A .tsrx file is scanned once, and its controls become legal TSX placeholders in a temporary in-memory copy. Your code is copied in unchanged.

steps.label: One parse
steps.caption: OXC parses that copy exactly once. There is no second parser and no TSRX fork of OXC.

steps.label: Your tree back
steps.caption: The tree is rebuilt into what you authored: controls like @for become real nodes, spans point at your bytes, and the four result fields load lazily.
